metadata.title: Basukinath to Deoghar via Trikut Parvat + Huge Peda Factory @ Ghormara + Samosi + Shringar/Aarti
metadata.description:
In this episode, we begin our journey from the sacred grounds of Baba Basukinath Temple, located around 45 km from Deoghar. Considered a key part of the pilgrimage circuit, the temple is visited by thousands of devotees every day, especially during the Shravani Mela. As we arrived, we were guided by a panda (temple priest), who helped us through the rituals. He performed a brief pooja and handed Anubhav a pot of holy water, which he carried into the sanctum to offer to the deity. The atmosphere was intense, a sea of devotees, chants echoing in the background, and a current of energy that made the experience unforgettable.

After the darshan, we wandered into the narrow bylanes surrounding the temple, known locally as Peda Gali. Lined with sweet shops and the aroma of khoya wafting through the air, it reminded us of the iconic peda gali near Baba Baidyanath Dham. Though smaller in scale, it had the same charm, people calling out their specialties, trays of fresh peda, and that old-town warmth.

Next, we started our street food trail with a stop at Marwari Basa, a simple eatery that serves both snacks and home-style meals. We opted for a plate of rice and dal, light, nourishing, and served with that unmistakable hospitality that small-town kitchens are known for.

Our food trail continued as we headed to Ghormara, a small town known for its legendary peda. Our destination was Sukhari Mandal Peda, believed to be the oldest peda shop in the area. The owner welcomed us warmly, shared the story of the shop, and even walked us through the peda-making process- boiling the milk, stirring the khoya, and shaping the peda by hand. We tasted it fresh, soft, milky, and gently sweet. A quiet moment of indulgence.

Just outside, we spotted a bhunja cart, run by a young man who kept his space remarkably neat. The mix of roasted grains, peanuts, and spices made for a crunchy, flavorful snack. We washed it down with a hot cup of chai from a nearby stall, a comforting pause in our journey.

From there, we made our way to Trikut Parvat, a scenic spot about 15 km from Deoghar. The hill is associated with mythology and is believed to be the meeting point of the three major Hindu deities, Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh. Though the ropeway was closed due to maintenance, the view of the hills and surrounding greenery offered a moment of calm after the hustle of the temples and markets.

As evening approached, we returned to Baba Baidyanath Dham for the Sandhya Aarti. Before entering, we stopped at the famous Dukhi Shah Dukan to try the Muni Samosa. Crisp on the outside, with a well-spiced potato filling, it was one of the best samosas we have had on this journey.

The episode closes with the powerful experience of Sandhya Aarti. It was a fitting end to a day filled with devotion, stories and simple food.
